title: Forms

learn.summary: Zinsser spends half of On Writing Well on forms — travel, memoir, science, sports, business — because principles only become skill inside a genre's specific demands. Each form has its own contract with the reader: the essay promises a mind at work, persuasion promises a fair case, narrative promises consequence, the work email promises brevity. Learn the contract before you improvise on it.

do: Pick the one form you use most in real life and write one deliberate, revised piece in it this week.

children.title: The Personal Essay

learn.summary: The essay descends from Montaigne, who coined the term from essayer, 'to attempt' — an attempt to think honestly on paper, using the self as evidence. The modern form's engine is the particular-to-universal move: a specific lived moment opened up until it says something true beyond the writer. The classic failure is staying private (a diary entry) or going abstract too fast (a sermon); the craft is holding both levels at once.

do: Write an 800-word essay starting from one specific memory of the past year, and make it earn one idea a stranger would care about.

children.title: Persuasive Writing

learn.summary: Aristotle's three appeals still organize the craft: ethos (credibility), logos (evidence and logic), pathos (emotion) — strong persuasion braids all three, weak persuasion leans on one. The modern power move is the steel man: stating the opposing case at full strength before answering it, which converts skeptics far better than strawmen. Structure matters too; op-ed editors want the claim within the first two paragraphs, not after a windup.

do: Write a 600-word op-ed on something you believe, including a full-strength paragraph for the other side that you then answer.

children.title: Storytelling & Narrative

learn.summary: Stories run on causality and stakes: 'the king died and then the queen died' is a chronicle; 'the queen died of grief' is a plot (E.M. Forster's distinction). The working kit is small — scene versus summary, concrete sensory detail, a character who wants something, and trouble in the way — and it transfers everywhere, from case studies to wedding toasts. Structure templates like the three-act arc are scaffolds, not laws.

do: Tell a true story from your life in exactly 300 words with one scene, one want, and one obstacle — then read it to someone and watch where they lean in.

children.title: Professional & Email Writing

learn.summary: Workplace writing is judged by the reader's clock: the subject line states the point, the first line states the ask, and anything past 150 words had better justify itself. BLUF (bottom line up front), scannable formatting, and one-topic-per-message are the norms plain-language research validates — US federal agencies are legally required to write this way under the Plain Writing Act of 2010. Kindness and clarity are not rivals; the clearest email is the most considerate one.

do: For one full week, put the ask in the first sentence of every work email and keep each under 150 words; note how reply speed changes.
